lines.text: Bear's Notes Why a Dim Blue Lamp Beats a
Blinding Red One
Aim the brightest red lamp you own at a
metal plate — and not one electron escapes.
Swap in a dim blue glow, and electrons fly
off the instant it lands.
Crank the red lamp up to blinding, pour on
more and more light — and still, nothing.
Brightness is energy, so more ought to mean more
— yet here it means nothing at all.
A wave washes its energy smoothly over every electron,
so enough brightness should eventually shake any one of
them loose.
But below a certain color, no brightness and no
patience ever free a single electron — so the
smooth-wave picture is simply wrong here.
So stop picturing a smooth wave, and picture light
arriving as separate packets.
Each packet carries a fixed energy set only by
its color — red packets weak, blue packets strong.
Turn up the brightness and you get more packets
per second, never fatter ones.
Every electron sits in the metal behind a fixed
escape cost it must be handed all at once
to break free.
And a packet is swallowed whole by one electron
— never shared as sips among many.
A weak red packet lands, falls short of the
escape cost, and its energy just bleeds away as
heat.
Pour on millions of red packets and every one
still falls short — a flood of near-misses frees
nothing.
Now one faint blue packet lands, clears the escape
cost in a single hit, and an electron flies
free.
Whatever energy is left after paying the cost becomes
that electron's speed.
So a packet's energy is just a constant times
its frequency — write it E equals h nu
— and that packet of light has a name:
a photon.
An electron escapes only when h nu beats the
cost, and the leftover is its kinetic energy:
K equals h nu minus the escape cost.
Below the frequency where h nu exactly equals the
cost, no packet can ever pay — that's the
threshold color.
Now the mystery dissolves:
brightness only counts the packets, but color decides whether
any single packet can pay.
A blinding red lamp is a torrent of packets
that each fall short;
a dim blue lamp is a trickle that each
clear the bar.
On sodium, ultraviolet at three hundred nanometers brings four
point one electron volts against a two point three
cost, and electrons leave with energy to spare.
Slide to green, and each packet lands a hair
below the cost — now not one electron leaves,
not even under a ten thousand watt lamp.
We didn't measure the constant h itself, or ask
how one packet can also behave like a wave
— each is its own video.
Try it yourself:
look up a metal's escape cost and find the
longest wavelength of light that can still free an
electron.
Thanks for watching Why a Dim Blue Lamp Beats
a Blinding Red One — more at youtube dot
com, slash, at Nik Bear Brown.
